_comment: Personal pronouns drawn as a picture, not searched for and not clozed (tunatale-3rxu, the user 2026-09-28). Each maps a word to a language-neutral concept in app.cards.pronoun_scenes.PRONOUN_CONCEPTS; the picture is a conversation with the referent filled and standing outside the outline, because a pronoun's meaning IS a relation between people and a photo cannot carry one. A word listed here is NOT a function word, whatever `function_words.json` or a POS tag says: app.srs.function_words.is_function_word vetoes it, so a PRON never goes down the case-marker cloze route. The veto is asked about a bare token, so listing a homograph would take EVERY sense of it off the picture route — the picture is therefore only drawn when the card's English gloss names the referent (app.cards.pronoun_picture.gloss_matches). Map only words whose MAIN sense is the personal pronoun. `kita` is also the root of 'to see' and of `kitaon` ('let's'), which is the one live homograph in this file: the token veto would have taken every sense of it off the picture route, so it is listed and the GLOSS guard does the separating instead — a `kita` glossed 'see' gets no picture. `siya` maps to third_one and carries NO gender mark. `kita` is the inclusive we and `kami` the exclusive one, the same distinction Tagalog draws. The `_poss` words are the FREE FORMS of the possessive (tunatale-uy38): the same conversation scene as their nominative, with a bag carried by every lit referent, which is what keeps `siya` ('he/she') and `niya` ('his/her') two different words on two different pictures. `ko` ('his/her') and `mo` ('my/our') are NOT here on purpose, and neither is `ka` ('your/yours'): each is an enclitic whose free form above already carries the same meaning, so the enclitic is drilled as a cloze and the free form gets the picture — listing both would put one meaning on two pictures and take the enclitic off the cloze route and back on again. `ka` is additionally in `function_words.json`'s include list, where a listing would be dead data. `niya` is the gender-neutral 'his/her' and takes the third_one_poss picture, which is the only place the possessive says which referent it is: the gloss decides, since the scene is the same for all of them.
